extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political economy, and social-science methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating sociological inquiry: when to use direct deduction versus the inverse (historical) method, how to form empirical laws from statistics/history, limits of abstraction, and how to verify social-scientific theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-deductive conclusions are tendencies not precise predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociology, when treated as a system of deductions à priori, cannot give positive predictions but only tendencies: we can conclude that a cause will operate in a certain manner unless counteracted, but cannot be assured to what extent or amount it will operate or that it will not be counteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive reasoning to identify directional tendencies; do not expect exact quantitative predictions because many coexisting agencies and unknown influences alter outcomes. Treat deductive results as guidance for action (e.g., to increase beneficial tendencies and counteract harmful ones) rather than infallible forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intermixture of causes (consensus of social phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every social phenomenon is more or less influenced by every other part of the social state; causes spread through society and contact different sets of agencies, producing modified effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid isolating social phenomena without careful justification. Recognize that to understand or change any one aspect of society you must consider its relations to other elements (the 'consensus' among social phenomena). When comparing societies, ensure their influencing circumstances and histories are comparable before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit direct-deductive inquiry to phenomena chiefly influenced by a few causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive methods must be confined to classes of social facts which, though influenced by many agents, are immediately determined principally by a few causes; otherwise hypothetical combinations become too complex and conclusions lose value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify phenomena where one class of immediate causes predominates. If the set of assumed circumstances is made too complex, error accumulates rapidly; keep hypotheses simple enough that the primary causes can be treated singly or in limited combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify creation of separate branches when immediate causes form a coherent class
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate branches (e.g., Political Economy) are warranted when a large class of social phenomena depends mainly, in the first resort, on one class of causes, so that their laws can be studied separately and later corrected for other influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When carving out a specialized science, ensure the phenomena chosen are primarily governed by a distinct set of causes. Treat the specialized science as conditional: its conclusions apply subject to later modification by the rest of the general social science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological abstraction in political economy (treat desire of wealth as sole motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Economy proceeds by treating mankind as if the desire of wealth were the sole motive (except the two perpetual counter-motives: aversion to labour and desire of present enjoyment) in domains where acquisition and distribution of wealth are the main concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simplifying hypothesis of exclusive wealth-seeking to derive tractable laws (e.g., on rent, wages, profits) and then correct these results by allowing for other motives when applying to real societies. Be explicit about what motives are abstracted away and when corrections are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise locally-derived conclusions before applying them to different societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic or social propositions drawn from one society (e.g., England) require revision when applied to societies with fundamentally different institutions, property relations, or distributions of capital and land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always trace back the premises of any conclusion and replace them with the premises appropriate to the target society. Avoid naively transplanting conclusions; instead derive analogous arguments from the correct premises for the new context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct general propositions as conditional (hypothetical) statements
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions in deductive social science are hypothetical: they are grounded on some supposed set of circumstances and declare how a cause would operate under those circumstances, with truth contingent on absence of modifying influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State assumptions explicitly. To approach concrete truth, increase the number of individualizing circumstances in the computation, but be wary of increasing complexity that magnifies uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistics and historical empirical laws to provide data for deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws derivable from statistics and history are needed to prepare observed facts for comparison with theoretical deductions; collecting such generalizations is an important part of sociological inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather and analyze statistical regularities where available; treat them as approximate generalizations to be used as data for deductive reasoning. Recognize their limited scope and approximate nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer causes indirectly from effects only with caution about remoter causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When immediate causes of social facts are not directly observable, their empirical laws may be inferred through their effects, but these inferences hold only so long as remoter causes (on which immediate causes depend) remain unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying cause-inferences from effects to new cases, investigate remoter causes and ensure no relevant change has occurred. Do not assume empirical inferences are universally transferable without this check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of direct verification in complex social interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For many social interventions (e.g., corn laws, prohibitive commercial systems) the effect of one cause is so masked by other simultaneous influences that specific experience cannot provide clear empirical laws or exact verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expecting direct experimental verification from historical trials in different societies or eras; individual instances are rarely exact matches. Instead rely on indirect methods of verification (see related criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect verification through successful explanation of other instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct verification is impossible, theory is indirectly verified by its ability to explain and predict other individual cases drawn from the same laws; experience that comes too late for a particular prediction can still corroborate the general theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test theories by checking whether they would have enabled explanation of already observed phenomena across a range of instances. Theories gain credibility if they account for multiple independent facts that they are supposed to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of retrodiction/explanation as the test of predictive competence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that our science makes us competent to predict the future in a given case, we must show it would have enabled us to predict the present and past; inability to account for existing facts indicates missing causes or inadequate theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying a theory to guide policy, demonstrate that it can account for the present state's relevant phenomena. If residual unexplained phenomena remain, either search for omitted circumstances or extend/improve the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit separate-science formation when ethological (character) influences are primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate departments should be created only when ethological differences (national or collective character) enter as secondary influences; where ethological factors are mixed up at every step, separate treatment is disadvantageous and such topics must remain within the general science of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the qualities of a people fundamentally shape the phenomena under study. If they do, integrate those inquiries with political ethology rather than isolating them into a separate science (e.g., do not treat 'Science of Government' separately when national character is central).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political ethology as a central, undeveloped branch requiring attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of causes that determine the type of character of a people (political ethology) is more important than many subordinate branches, because national character both results from and causally influences other social phenomena; yet it is in its infancy and must be developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize study of how institutions and social arrangements shape and are shaped by national character. Incorporate ethological laws when applying conclusions from specialized branches (e.g., political economy) to different national contexts.
